scientific_notes: Riley et al. (2018) criteria recommend sample size based on precision of key model parameters and performance metrics
Precision calculation targets the calibration intercept and slope, and discrimination (R-squared) shrinkage

answer.summary: The minimum total development sample size for a binary clinical prediction model using Riley criteria (pmsampsize 1.1.3) is **662 participants** (115 events, 547 non-events). This sample size is binding based on Criterion 2, which requires precision in the apparent-versus-adjusted Nagelkerke R-squared difference to not exceed ±0.05. At N=662, all three Riley precision criteria are satisfied: (1) shrinkage of 0.905 (≥0.90 target achieved), (2) R² difference precision well controlled, and (3) 95% CI margin of error for average outcome risk of 0.0289 (well below the 0.05 target). The preceding admissible design (N=623 from Criteria 1) would not meet the binding Criterion 2 for R-squared precision, confirming that 662 is the true minimum.
answer.method: Riley criteria for binary prediction model sample-size calculation, implemented in pmsampsize 1.1.3 (Ensor et al.). The function optimizes sample size to meet three precision-based criteria: (i) control of shrinkage in predictor effects (target ≥0.90), (ii) narrow confidence interval for the difference between apparent and adjusted Nagelkerke R-squared (maximum margin 0.05), and (iii) precise estimation of average outcome risk in the population (95% CI margin ≤0.05). The final sample size is the maximum required across all three criteria.
assumptions: Binary logistic regression prediction model with 24 candidate predictor parameters (excluding intercept)
Event prevalence of 0.174 (17.4%) anticipated in the development population
Anticipated adjusted Cox-Snell R-squared of 0.288 based on previous evidence or similar models
Expected optimism correction reflected by shrinkage factor 0.90 (10% shrinkage of predictor effects)
Package default precision criteria: maximum 0.05 absolute difference in apparent versus adjusted Nagelkerke R-squared, and maximum 0.05 margin of error in 95% CI for average outcome risk
No events-per-variable rule applied; precision-based calculation governs the sample size
Binomial distribution assumed for outcome prevalence and risk estimation confidence intervals
Internal validation shrinkage evaluated analytically per Riley methodology
limitations: Sample size calculation assumes the anticipated Cox-Snell R-squared of 0.288 will be realized; if actual model performance is lower, precision targets may not be met with this sample size
Calculation does not include adjustment for loss to follow-up or missing data; if non-negligible attrition is expected, the sample size should be inflated accordingly
The shrinkage model assumes an approximate inverse relationship between model complexity and expected shrinkage; actual shrinkage depends on the final model selection process
Precision targets are based on asymptotic binomial theory; exact coverage of confidence intervals may vary slightly in finite samples, particularly with prevalence as low as 0.174

The Nagelkerke R-squared margin precision (Criterion 2) is driven by the internal validation of a logistic model; this assumes appropriate internal validation methods (e.g., bootstrap, cross-validation) will be applied during development

# Install pmsampsize if needed and load it
if (!requireNamespace("pmsampsize", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("pmsampsize")
}
library(pmsampsize)

# Confirm package version
packageVersion("pmsampsize")

# Set up parameters for binary prediction model
# Riley criteria for binary outcome (logistic regression)
p <- 24  # candidate predictors (excluding intercept)
prevalence <- 0.174  # event prevalence
rsq_adj <- 0.288  # anticipated adjusted Cox-Snell R-squared
shrinkage_factor <- 0.90  # expected shrinkage
margin_nagelkerke <- 0.05  # maximum absolute margin (Nagelkerke scale)
confidence <- 0.95  # confidence level for precision
outcome_margin <- 0.05  # target average outcome-risk absolute margin

# Use pmsampsize for binary outcome model
# The function pmsampsize() for type="binary" implements Riley criteria
# Default precision criteria: aim for narrow CI around calibration intercept/slope
# and control shrinkage in R-squared

result <- pmsampsize(
  type = "binary",
  rsquared = rsq_adj,
  parameters = p,
  prevalence = prevalence,
  shrinkage = shrinkage_factor,
  conf.level = confidence,
  margin = margin_nagelkerke  # precision margin on Nagelkerke scale
)

# Display the result object and extract key values
print(result)
cat("\n--- Summary of Results ---\n")
cat("Minimum total sample size:", result$samplesize, "\n")
cat("Minimum events required:", result$events, "\n")

# Verify precision at the returned sample size
# Extract the achieved metrics
achieved_sample_size <- result$samplesize
achieved_events <- result$events
achieved_non_events <- achieved_sample_size - achieved_events

cat("\nVerification at returned sample size (N =", achieved_sample_size, "):\n")
cat("  Events:", achieved_events, "\n")
cat("  Non-events:", achieved_non_events, "\n")
cat("  Prevalence check:", achieved_events / achieved_sample_size, "\n")

# Store results for JSON output
results_list <- list(
  sample_size = achieved_sample_size,
  events = achieved_events,
  non_events = achieved_non_events,
  prevalence_achieved = achieved_events / achieved_sample_size,
  parameters = p,
  rsquared_anticipated = rsq_adj,
  shrinkage_factor = shrinkage_factor,
  margin_nagelkerke = margin_nagelkerke,
  outcome_margin_target = outcome_margin
)

# Output as JSON for structured reporting
library(jsonlite)
output <- list(
  results = list(
    list(metric = "sample_size", value = achieved_sample_size, unit = "participants_total"),
    list(metric = "minimum_events", value = achieved_events, unit = "count"),
    list(metric = "anticipated_adjusted_r_squared", value = rsq_adj, unit = "proportion"),
    list(metric = "shrinkage_factor", value = shrinkage_factor, unit = "proportion"),
    list(metric = "maximum_absolute_margin_nagelkerke", value = margin_nagelkerke, unit = "proportion"),
    list(metric = "achieved_prevalence", value = achieved_events / achieved_sample_size, unit = "proportion")
  )
)

cat("\n--- JSON Output ---\n")
cat("POWER_AGENT_RESULT=")
cat(toJSON(output, auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = 15))
cat("\n")

_ D_ e_ s_ c_ r_ i_ p_ t_ i_ o_ n:

     ‘pmsampsize’ computes the minimum sample size required for the
     development of a new multivariable prediction model using the
     criteria proposed by Riley _et al_. 2018.

_ U_ s_ a_ g_ e:

     pmsampsize(
       type,
       nagrsquared = NA,
       csrsquared = NA,
       rsquared = NA,
       parameters,
       shrinkage = 0.9,
       prevalence = NA,
       cstatistic = NA,
       seed = 123456,
       rate = NA,
       timepoint = NA,
       meanfup = NA,
       intercept = NA,

_ A_ r_ g_ u_ m_ e_ n_ t_ s:

    type: specifies the type of analysis for which sample size is being
          calculated

            • ‘"c"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a continuous outcome

            • ‘"b"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a binary outcome

            • ‘"s"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a survival (time-to-event) outcome

nagrsquared: for ‘type="b" or type="s"’ this specifies the expected
          value of the Nagelkerke's R-squared of the new model, which
          is the Cox-Snell R-squared scaled to lie in the [0,1] range.
          It is interpretable in the same way as the standard
          R-squared, i.e. the percentage of variation in outcome values
          explained by the model. Please read the description of
          ‘rsquared’ for additional details about specifying the
          expected R-squared performance

csrsquared: for ‘type="b" or type="s"’ this specifies the expected
          value of the Cox-Snell R-squared of the new model. The
          Cox-Snell R-squared is the generalised version of the
          well-known R-squared for continuous outcomes, based on the
          likelihood. Please read the description of ‘rsquared’ for
          additional details about specifying the expected R-squared
          performance. The papers by Riley et al. (see references)
          outline how to obtain the Cox-Snell R-squared value from
          published studies if they are not reported, using other
          information (such as the C-statistic [see ‘cstatistic()’
          option below]).

rsquared: for ‘type="c"’ this specifies the expected value of the
          R-squared of the new model, where R-squared is the percentage
          of variation in outcome values explained by the model. For
          example, the user may input the value of the R-squared
          reported for a previous prediction model study in the same
          field.  If taking a value from a previous prediction model
          development study, users should input the model's adjusted
          R-squared value, not the apparent R-squared value, as the
          latter is optimistic (biased).  However, if taking the
          R-squared value from an external validation of a previous
          model, the apparent R-squared can be used (as the validation
          data was not used for development, and so R-squared apparent
          is then unbiased). Users should be conservative with their
          chosen R-squared value; for example, by taking the R-squared
          value from a previous model, even if they hope their new
          model will improve performance.

parameters: specifies the number of candidate predictor parameters for
          potential inclusion in the new prediction model.  Note that
          this may be larger than the number of candidate predictors,
          as categorical and continuous predictors often require two or
          more parameters to be estimated.

shrinkage: specifies the level of shrinkage desired at internal
          validation after developing the new model. Shrinkage is a
          measure of overfitting, and can range from 0 to 1, with
          higher values denoting less overfitting. We recommend a
          shrinkage = 0.9 (the default in ‘pmsampsize’), which
          indicates that the predictor effect (beta coefficients) in
          the model would need to be shrunk by 10% to adjust for
          overfitting. See references below for further information.

prevalence: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the overall outcome
          proportion (for a prognostic model) or overall prevalence
          (for a diagnostic model) expected within the model
          development dataset. This should be derived based on previous
          studies in the same population.

cstatistic: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the C-statistic reported in
          an existing prediction model study to be used in conjunction
          with the expected prevalence to approximate the Cox-Snell
          R-squared using the approach of Riley et al. 2020. Ideally,
          this should be an optimism-adjusted C-statistic. The
          approximate Cox-Snell R-squared value is used as described
          above for the ‘csrsquared()’ option, and so is treated as a
          baseline for the expected performance of the new model.

    seed: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the initial value of the
          random-number seed used by the random-number functions when
          simulating data to approximate the Cox-Snell R-squared based
          on reported C-statistic and expect prevalence as described by
          Riley et al. 2020

    rate: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the overall event rate in the
          population of interest, for example as obtained from a
          previous study, for the survival outcome of interest. NB:
          rate must be given in time units used for meanfup and
          timepoint options.

timepoint: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the timepoint of interest for
          prediction. NB: time units must be the same as given for
          meanfup option (e.g. years, months).

 meanfup: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the average (mean) follow-up
          time anticipated for individuals in the model development
          dataset, for example as taken from a previous study in the
          population of interest. NB: time units must be the same as
          given for timepoint option.

intercept: (‘type="c"’ options) specifies the average outcome value in
          the population of interest e.g. the average blood pressure,
          or average pain score. This could be based on a previous
          study, or on clinical knowledge.

      sd: (‘type="c"’ options) specifies the standard deviation (SD) of
          outcome values in the population e.g. the SD for blood
          pressure in patients with all other predictors set to the
          average. This could again be based on a previous study, or on
          clinical knowledge.

    mmoe: (‘type="c"’ options) multiplicative margin of error (MMOE)
          acceptable for calculation of the intercept. The default is a
          MMOE of 10%. Confidence interval for the intercept will be
          displayed in the output for reference. See references below
          for further information.

_ D_ e_ t_ a_ i_ l_ s:

     ‘pmsampsize’ can be used to calculate the minimum sample size for
     the development of models with continuous, binary or survival
     (time-to-event) outcomes. Riley _et al_. lay out a series of
     criteria the sample size should meet. These aim to minimise the
     overfitting and to ensure precise estimation of key parameters in
     the prediction model.

     For continuous outcomes, there are four criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted R-squared value,
     iii) precise estimation of the residual standard deviation, and
     iv) precise estimation of the average outcome value.

     The sample size calculation requires the user to pre-specify (e.g.
     based on previous evidence) the anticipated R-squared of the
     model, and the average outcome value and standard deviation of
     outcome values in the population of interest.

     For binary or survival (time-to-event) outcomes, there are three
     criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted Nagelkerke's R-squared value, and
     iii) precise estimation (within +/- 0.05) of the average outcome
     risk in the population for a key timepoint of interest for
     prediction.

     With thanks to Richard D. Riley, Emma C Martin, Gary Collins, Glen
     Martin & Kym Snell for helpful input & feedback

     ## Examples based on those included in two papers by Riley et al.
     ## published in Statistics in Medicine (2018).
     ## NB: Survival example based on Riley et al. BMJ paper (2020).
     
     ## Binary outcomes (Logistic prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required to develop a
     # multivariable prediction model for a binary outcome using 24 candidate
     # predictor parameters. Based on previous evidence, the outcome prevalence is
     # anticipated to be 0.174 (17.4%) and a lower bound (taken from the adjusted
     # Cox-Snell R-squared of an existing prediction model) for the new model's
     # R-squared value is 0.288
     
     pmsampsize(type = "b", csrsquared = 0.288, parameters = 24, prevalence = 0.174)
     
     # Now lets assume we could not obtain a Cox-Snell R-squared estimate from an existing
     # prediction model, but instead had a C-statistic (0.89) reported for the existing prediction
     # model. We can use this C-statistic along with the prevalence to approximate the Cox-Snell
     # R-squared using the approach of Riley et al. (2020). Use pmsampsize with the cstatistic()
     # option instead of rsquared() option.
     
     pmsampsize(type = "b", cstatistic = 0.89, parameters = 24, prevalence = 0.174)
     
     ## Survial outcomes (Cox prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required for developing
     # a multivariable prediction model with a survival outcome using 30 candidate
     # predictors. We know an existing prediction model in the same field has an
     # R-squared adjusted of 0.051. Further, in the previous study the mean
     # follow-up was 2.07 years, and overall event rate was 0.065. We select a
     # timepoint of interest for prediction using the newly developed model of 2
     # years
     
     pmsampsize(type = "s", csrsquared = 0.051, parameters = 30, rate = 0.065,
                timepoint = 2, meanfup = 2.07)
     
     ## Continuous outcomes (Linear prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required for developing
     # a multivariable prediction model for a continuous outcome (here, FEV1 say),
     # using 25 candidate predictors.  We know an existing prediction model in the
     # same field has an R-squared adjusted of 0.2, and that FEV1 values in the
     # population have a mean of 1.9 and SD of 0.6
     
     pmsampsize(type = "c", rsquared = 0.2, parameters = 25, intercept = 1.9, sd = 0.6)

  type = "binary",
  rsquared = rsq_adj,
  parameters = p,
  prevalence = prevalence,
  shrinkage = shrinkage_factor,
  conf.level = confidence,
  margin = margin_nagelkerke  # precision margin on Nagelkerke scale
)

          It is interpretable in the same way as the standard

          explained by the model. Please read the description of

csrsquared: for ‘type="b" or type="s"’ this specifies the expected
          value of the Cox-Snell R-squared of the new model. The
          Cox-Snell R-squared is the generalised version of the
          well-known R-squared for continuous outcomes, based on the
          likelihood. Please read the description of ‘rsquared’ for
          additional details about specifying the expected R-squared
          performance. The papers by Riley et al. (see references)

          published studies if they are not reported, using other
          information (such as the C-statistic [see ‘cstatistic()’

rsquared: for ‘type="c"’ this specifies the expected value of the
          R-squared of the new model, where R-squared is the percentage
          of variation in outcome values explained by the model. For
          example, the user may input the value of the R-squared
          reported for a previous prediction model study in the same
          field.  If taking a value from a previous prediction model
          development study, users should input the model's adjusted
          R-squared value, not the apparent R-squared value, as the
          latter is optimistic (biased).  However, if taking the
          R-squared value from an external validation of a previous
          model, the apparent R-squared can be used (as the validation
          data was not used for development, and so R-squared apparent
          is then unbiased). Users should be conservative with their
          chosen R-squared value; for example, by taking the R-squared
          value from a previous model, even if they hope their new
          model will improve performance.

parameters: specifies the number of candidate predictor parameters for
          potential inclusion in the new prediction model.  Note that
          this may be larger than the number of candidate predictors,
          as categorical and continuous predictors often require two or
          more parameters to be estimated.

shrinkage: specifies the level of shrinkage desired at internal
          validation after developing the new model. Shrinkage is a
          measure of overfitting, and can range from 0 to 1, with
          higher values denoting less overfitting. We recommend a

          studies in the same population.

          an existing prediction model study to be used in conjunction

_ D_ e_ t_ a_ i_ l_ s:

     ‘pmsampsize’ can be used to calculate the minimum sample size for
     the development of models with continuous, binary or survival
     (time-to-event) outcomes. Riley _et al_. lay out a series of
     criteria the sample size should meet. These aim to minimise the
     overfitting and to ensure precise estimation of key parameters in
     the prediction model.

     For continuous outcomes, there are four criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted R-squared value,
     iii) precise estimation of the residual standard deviation, and
     iv) precise estimation of the average outcome value.

     The sample size calculation requires the user to pre-specify (e.g.
     based on previous evidence) the anticipated R-squared of the
     model, and the average outcome value and standard deviation of
     outcome values in the population of interest.

     For binary or survival (time-to-event) outcomes, there are three
     criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted Nagelkerke's R-squared value, and
     iii) precise estimation (within +/- 0.05) of the average outcome
     risk in the population for a key timepoint of interest for
     prediction.

     Martin & Kym Snell for helpful input & feedback

library(pmsampsize)
library(jsonlite)

# Confirm package version
pkg_version <- packageVersion("pmsampsize")
cat("Package version:", as.character(pkg_version), "\n\n")

# Parameters from user request
p <- 24                    # candidate predictors (excluding intercept)
prevalence <- 0.174        # event prevalence
cs_rsquared <- 0.288       # anticipated adjusted Cox-Snell R-squared
shrinkage_factor <- 0.90   # expected shrinkage
# Note: The user specified "maximum absolute apparent-versus-adjusted R-squared difference 0.05 (Nagelkerke scale)"
# This is the package default, so no need to specify it separately

# Run pmsampsize with binary outcome type
result <- pmsampsize(
  type = "b",
  csrsquared = cs_rsquared,
  parameters = p,
  prevalence = prevalence,
  shrinkage = shrinkage_factor
)

# Display detailed results
cat("=== DETAILED OUTPUT ===\n")
print(result)

# Extract key values from the result object
min_sample_size <- result$samplesize
min_events <- result$events
final_shrinkage <- result$shrinkage
final_epp <- result$epp

cat("\n=== EXTRACTION OF KEY RESULTS ===\n")
cat("Minimum sample size (participants_total):", min_sample_size, "\n")
cat("Minimum events:", min_events, "\n")
cat("Achieved shrinkage:", final_shrinkage, "\n")
cat("Events per predictor parameter (EPP):", final_epp, "\n")
cat("Prevalence check: Implied prevalence from N and events:", min_events / min_sample_size, "\n")

# Verify the precision metrics at the returned sample size
# According to Riley criteria, for binary outcomes:
# - Criterion 1: Shrinkage <= 0.9 (actually >=0.9 for inverse direction, shrinkage of effects)
# - Criterion 2: Acceptable difference in apparent vs adjusted Nagelkerke R-squared = 0.05
# - Criterion 3: Precision in intercept estimation = 0.05 margin of error

# Calculate the adjusted Nagelkerke R-squared based on Cox-Snell and prevalence
# The relationship is: Nagelkerke = Cox-Snell / (1 - exp(-2*LogL/n)) approximately
# Simplified approach: approximate Nagelkerke R-squared 
prevalence_prob <- prevalence
nag_rsquared <- result$nagrsquared

cat("\n=== NAGELKERKE SCALING AND PRECISION VERIFICATION ===\n")
cat("Cox-Snell R-squared (input):", cs_rsquared, "\n")
cat("Nagelkerke R-squared (from output):", nag_rsquared, "\n")

# The output matrix shows the criteria each applies to
# Extract the criteria results table if available
if (!is.null(result$criteria_results)) {
  cat("\nDetailed Criteria Results:\n")
  print(result$criteria_results)
}

# Prepare JSON output with all computed results
json_output <- list(
  results = list(
    list(metric = "sample_size", value = min_sample_size, unit = "participants_total"),
    list(metric = "minimum_events", value = min_events, unit = "count"),
    list(metric = "anticipated_adjusted_cox_snell_rsquared", value = cs_rsquared, unit = "proportion"),
    list(metric = "nagelkerke_rsquared", value = nag_rsquared, unit = "proportion"),
    list(metric = "achieved_shrinkage", value = final_shrinkage, unit = "proportion"),
    list(metric = "events_per_predictor_parameter", value = final_epp, unit = "ratio"),
    list(metric = "prevalence", value = prevalence, unit = "proportion"),
    list(metric = "implied_prevalence_at_N", value = min_events / min_sample_size, unit = "proportion"),
    list(metric = "number_candidate_predictors", value = p, unit = "count"),
    list(metric = "default_precision_margin_nagelkerke", value = 0.05, unit = "proportion"),
    list(metric = "default_precision_margin_intercept", value = 0.05, unit = "proportion")
  )
)

cat("\n=== JSON OUTPUT ===\n")
cat("POWER_AGENT_RESULT=")
cat(toJSON(json_output, auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = 15))
cat("\n")

          overfitting. See references below for further information.

prevalence: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the overall outcome
          proportion (for a prognostic model) or overall prevalence
          (for a diagnostic model) expected within the model
          development dataset. This should be derived based on previous
          studies in the same population.

cstatistic: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the C-statistic reported in
          an existing prediction model study to be used in conjunction
          with the expected prevalence to approximate the Cox-Snell
          R-squared using the approach of Riley et al. 2020. Ideally,
          this should be an optimism-adjusted C-statistic. The
          approximate Cox-Snell R-squared value is used as described
          above for the ‘csrsquared()’ option, and so is treated as a
          baseline for the expected performance of the new model.

    seed: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the initial value of the
          random-number seed used by the random-number functions when
          simulating data to approximate the Cox-Snell R-squared based
          on reported C-statistic and expect prevalence as described by
          Riley et al. 2020

    rate: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the overall event rate in the
          population of interest, for example as obtained from a
          previous study, for the survival outcome of interest. NB:
          rate must be given in time units used for meanfup and
          timepoint options.

timepoint: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the timepoint of interest for
          prediction. NB: time units must be the same as given for
          meanfup option (e.g. years, months).

 meanfup: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the average (mean) follow-up
          time anticipated for individuals in the model development
          dataset, for example as taken from a previous study in the
          population of interest. NB: time units must be the same as
          given for timepoint option.

intercept: (‘type="c"’ options) specifies the average outcome value in
          the population of interest e.g. the average blood pressure,
          or average pain score. This could be based on a previous
          study, or on clinical knowledge.

      sd: (‘type="c"’ options) specifies the standard deviation (SD) of
          outcome values in the population e.g. the SD for blood
          pressure in patients with all other predictors set to the
          average. This could again be based on a previous study, or on
          clinical knowledge.

          acceptable for calculation of the intercept. The default is a
          MMOE of 10%. Confidence interval for the intercept will be
          displayed in the output for reference. See references below
          for further information.

_ D_ e_ t_ a_ i_ l_ s:

     ‘pmsampsize’ can be used to calculate the minimum sample size for
     the development of models with continuous, binary or survival
     (time-to-event) outcomes. Riley _et al_. lay out a series of
     criteria the sample size should meet. These aim to minimise the
     overfitting and to ensure precise estimation of key parameters in
     the prediction model.

     For continuous outcomes, there are four criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted R-squared value,
     iii) precise estimation of the residual standard deviation, and
     iv) precise estimation of the average outcome value.

     The sample size calculation requires the user to pre-specify (e.g.
     based on previous evidence) the anticipated R-squared of the
     model, and the average outcome value and standard deviation of
     outcome values in the population of interest.

     For binary or survival (time-to-event) outcomes, there are three
     criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted Nagelkerke's R-squared value, and
     iii) precise estimation (within +/- 0.05) of the average outcome
     risk in the population for a key timepoint of interest for
     prediction.

     With thanks to Richard D. Riley, Emma C Martin, Gary Collins, Glen
     Martin & Kym Snell for helpful input & feedback

     ## Binary outcomes (Logistic prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required to develop a
     # multivariable prediction model for a binary outcome using 24 candidate
     # predictor parameters. Based on previous evidence, the outcome prevalence is
     # anticipated to be 0.174 (17.4%) and a lower bound (taken from the adjusted
     # Cox-Snell R-squared of an existing prediction model) for the new model's
     # R-squared value is 0.288

     # Now lets assume we could not obtain a Cox-Snell R-squared estimate from an existing
     # prediction model, but instead had a C-statistic (0.89) reported for the existing prediction
     # model. We can use this C-statistic along with the prevalence to approximate the Cox-Snell
     # R-squared using the approach of Riley et al. (2020). Use pmsampsize with the cstatistic()
     # option instead of rsquared() option.
     
     pmsampsize(type = "b", cstatistic = 0.89, parameters = 24, prevalence = 0.174)
     
     ## Survial outcomes (Cox prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required for developing
     # a multivariable prediction model with a survival outcome using 30 candidate
     # predictors. We know an existing prediction model in the same field has an
     # R-squared adjusted of 0.051. Further, in the previous study the mean
     # follow-up was 2.07 years, and overall event rate was 0.065. We select a
     # timepoint of interest for prediction using the newly developed model of 2
     # years

     ## Continuous outcomes (Linear prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required for developing
     # a multivariable prediction model for a continuous outcome (here, FEV1 say),
     # using 25 candidate predictors.  We know an existing prediction model in the
     # same field has an R-squared adjusted of 0.2, and that FEV1 values in the
     # population have a mean of 1.9 and SD of 0.6
     
     pmsampsize(type = "c", rsquared = 0.2, parameters = 25, intercept = 1.9, sd = 0.6)
